the total effect is 9. Regressing Y on all four inputs recovers the exact conditional equation,
but summing its action coefficients gives 7. The missing 2 is the effect of A0 mediated by L1 .
Omitting L1 instead confounds the A1 coefficient. Thus even a perfect conditional regression
requires the g-formula’s averaging operation to answer the sustained-intervention question.
  The example has no hidden confounding, perfect measurement and support for all action
paths. Its failure is entirely a target error. This is why the theoretical treatment must precede
a banking pilot: the problem can already be proved without institutional data.


5.4     Marginal structural models and structural nested models
A marginal structural model (MSM) parameterizes a collection of regime means, such as
E[Y a0 ,a1 ] = β0 + β1 a0 + β2 a1 + β12 a0 a1 . An estimator must account for the assignment
mechanism, rather than fit that marginal mean directly to the observed conditional outcome
law. For fixed ā,                  "                    #
                                       1{Ā = ā}
                                  E Q                   Y = E[Y ā ].
                                        t et (at | Ht )

Weighted estimating equations combine such identities across regimes. If the MSM is misspeci-
fied, the result is a projection determined by the chosen regime weights. Stabilized weights
with numerators depending on past actions create a different pseudopopulation; a correctly
specified MSM may retain its parameter, but a misspecified projection and its variance can
change. Weight clipping is another bias/variance choice, not a neutral algebraic transformation
(Hernán and Robins, 2020, Chapter 21).
   A structural nested mean model (SNMM) instead parameterizes the mean effect of a
treatment blip at a time, within the history and receipt strata at that time, with subsequent
treatment set to a reference regime. For two decisions and reference zero, define

                     γ1 (h1 , a1 ; β) = E[Y a0 ,a1 − Y a0 ,0 | H1 = h1 , A1 = a1 ],
                     γ0 (h0 , a0 ; β) = E[Y a0 ,0 − Y 0,0 | H0 = h0 , A0 = a0 ].               (5.5)

The conditioning is on histories compatible with the displayed past; these are mean contrasts
and need not specify each person’s effect. At the true parameter let U1 = Y − γ1 (H1 , A1 ; β)
and U0 = U1 − γ0 (H0 , A0 ; β). By the definition of γ1 , the conditional mean of U1 equals that
of Y A0 ,0 . Sequential exchangeability makes that mean invariant to A1 given H1 . Averaging
over the next history and removing γ0 then makes the mean of U0 invariant to A0 given H0 .
Consequently, for appropriate history instruments dt (Ht ),

              E[dt (Ht ){At − et (1 | Ht )}{Ut (β) − E[Ut (β) | Ht ]}] = 0,        t = 0, 1.   (5.6)

These moment equations define a g-estimation strategy. Identification requires rank and a
correct blip model. The mean restriction does not assert that the blipped outcome equals
the individual’s no-treatment counterfactual, nor that it is conditionally independent of
treatment in its entire distribution. Those are stronger distributional or rank-preserving claims
(Vansteelandt and Joffe, 2014, Sections 3.2, 5 and 6.1).
  In the exact example above, γ1 = 4a1 and γ0 = 5a0 . The early blip includes the 2-unit
mediated effect, unlike the coefficient of A0 in the regression conditioning on L1 . These values
make the sequential residual moments vanish. Replacing the early blip by 3a0 leaves a nonzero
moment. Thus g-estimation’s causal parameter is visible in a checkable moment calculation.
  The relationship with IV is now precise. In Chapter 2, a valid instrument supplies a residual
moment for an endogenous receipt. Under sequential exchangeability, the residual of the action
34                                                                              Causal analysis for a universal bank


mechanism supplies a moment after later effects have been removed. Structural nested IV
variants replace ignorability with other restrictions; their identified blip parameters need not
identify arbitrary marginal regime means. An MSM, an SNMM and a predictive state-space
model are different models of different objects, even when all use linear functions.

5.6     Observation, censoring and eligibility are mechanisms
Suppose Ct+1 = 1 means the next observation is retained, with πt = P (Ct+1 = 1 | Ht , At , Ct =

This is a second mechanism replacement: it emulates retaining the defined outcome. It does
not emulate preventing default, death or another event that changes what the endpoint means.
Re-entry, debt sale, account closure and competing events need separate clocks and targets.
Eligibility Et affected by prior actions belongs in Ht and in the feasible action set. Restricting
retrospectively to people eligible at every time selects on post-treatment history. A policy
must specify what happens on ineligible histories rather than delete them silently.


5.7     A controlled state-space model on the same clock
Now suppose the relevant condition is a hidden state St and the bank observes a signal Ot before
acting. Let Ht = (O0 , A0 , R0 , O1 , . . . , At−1 , Rt−1 , Ot ). A particular controlled model supplies
initial law µθ , initial emission B0,θ , transition Pθ (s′ | s, a), reward density Fθ (r | s, a, s′ ), and
next signal density Bθ (o′ | s′ , a). This last conditional-independence structure is a model
restriction. A joint reward/signal density is needed if those emissions are not conditionally
independent as specified.
   Let qη (a | s, h) represent behavior, possibly using private information summarized by s.
With other time-varying inputs understood as explicit arguments, the complete trajectory law

The observed likelihood sums this law over the hidden states. A causal interpretation further
requires the state-transition, reward and signal mechanisms to remain invariant when the action
mechanism is replaced, with state sufficient to capture relevant hidden dependence. Those
restrictions can be expressed by a time-indexed SCM with mutually independent innovations
conditional on the declared state. A model fitted to the observational likelihood does not
prove that it is such an SCM.

  Under a target policy using only recorded history, replace the qη factor by gt (a | h). This
defines a model-conditional intervention law. Whether its value is identified from historical
observations is a separate question about the model class and information, to which we return
below. A private logger with memory not captured by St , Ht requires state augmentation or a
more general behavior kernel; the displayed finite-state model would otherwise be misspecified.


5.7.1     Recovering the observed-history g-formula

If qη (a | s, h) = et (a | h) and the structural innovations justify sequential exchangeability,
actions supply no extra information about St conditional on Ht . Summing Equation (5.14) over
states defines observable history kernels for (Rt , Ot+1 ). Under common supported histories,
their conditional state mixtures are invariant to replacing the observed-history policy, because
the action factors cancel from the latent posterior. Hence replacing et by gt yields the history
g-formula.
   This establishes the bridge: a controlled state-space model is a restricted parameterization
of longitudinal observation kernels when its action and observation assumptions permit that
reduction. It can be computationally valuable when histories are long. It is not a weaker
replacement for the causal assumptions underlying those kernels. When St is observed and
Markov sufficient, Qt (Ht , a) reduces to Qt (St , a); under partial observation it can reduce to a
belief state under further restrictions.

   If qη = eη (a | h) and its parameters are distinct from θ, its factors can be removed from

Future actions can depend on earlier observations. Conditioning on their whole sequence would
require a different normalization.
   Smoothing estimates P (St | HT ) and uses later information. It is useful for parameter
estimation and historical diagnosis, but is not a state available to the decision at t. Using
it as if it were a prospective policy input creates leakage. When parameters are uncertain,
a Bayesian sufficient state may be the joint posterior of (St , θ); plugging in θb produces a
conditional planning calculation and omits parameter-learning value and uncertainty.

Assume a known, invariant controlled Markov environment and a target policy using the full

Replacing the policy average by a maximum gives the finite-horizon planning recursion when
actions are feasible and rewards integrable. For a stationary discounted model with bounded
rewards and 0 < γ < 1, the optimal Bellman operator is a contraction in sup norm: the
difference of two maximized continuation values is at most γ∥V − W ∥∞ . This gives a unique
bounded fixed point. The belief-state sufficiency construction is developed in Kaelbling et al.
(1998, Sections 3.2–3.4); it assumes a supplied model.
   Three distinct identification questions precede causal use of the value. First, can the
observed law identify the likelihood parameters within the proposed state-space class? For
an uncontrolled stationary K-state HMM, full-rank ergodic transition and distinct emission
distributions identify parameters up to labels from a sufficiently long observation block under
the cited conditions (Alexandrovich et al., 2016, Theorem 1). This theorem is not automatically
a controlled, privately logged HMM theorem.
   Second, does the historical model identify the intervention law after changing q? Causal
autonomy, action support and restrictions on hidden assignment and measurement are ad-
ditional. Third, is the requested policy value uniquely determined even if some parameters
are not? Formally, for every two admissible models with the same observed law, one needs
VM1 (g) = VM2 (g), which is weaker than equality of every latent parameter but stronger than
good fit.
  A permutation of hidden-state labels leaves both observation likelihood and coherently
computed policy values unchanged; it is a representational ambiguity. The two worlds in
Chapter 1 instead have the same likelihood and different action values; that is causal ambiguity.
40                                                             Causal analysis for a universal bank


A bootstrap conditional on one selected model measures sampling variation within it and does
not cover the latter ambiguity. Specialized POMDP off-policy identification uses informative
proxies or other restrictions (Tennenholtz et al., 2020); it is not supplied by a generic filter or
by the contraction proof.


5.10      What a state-space adapter must preserve
A numerical filter consumes transition and observation kernels, initial state, parameter values
and masks. A causal adapter additionally needs the action clock, logger information, inter-
vention mechanism, reward definition and source of identification. It must specify whether
a missing measurement is exogenous, conditionally ignorable, or modeled through a state-
dependent observation process. Omitting an endogenous mask changes the likelihood and may
change policy identification.
   For continuous states, sums become integrals and Kalman, nonlinear Gaussian, particle or
variational methods approximate different objects. The state-space adapter should report the
actual likelihood approximation, not only the latent-state dimension. Label fixing, deterministic
lag coordinates, parameter priors and reward integration must be coherent across fitting and
intervention evaluation. This is how a numerical filtering library can be reused without
attributing causal guarantees to its numerical accuracy.
  The customer and the bank may also be different decision makers. The bank’s POMDP
maximizes a supplied bank reward. A model of customer activation, refinancing or default
requires utility, beliefs, information and transition restrictions of its own. Estimating a
customer’s dynamic choice likelihood is not equivalent to optimizing the bank’s reward;
equilibrium response adds another layer. Chapter 7 develops that inverse decision problem;
Chapters 9 and 12 connect structural shocks and feedback to it.
Chapter 6

Changing policies, censoring and
events that end a decision

The history g-formula identifies a specified intervention, not every quantity labeled a policy
effect. A bank may increase an existing offer probability, modify an employee’s proposed credit
limit, or stop making decisions after repayment. These operations use different information
and produce different statistical functionals. Their distinctions also determine which nuisance
functions enter an influence function.


6.1    Incremental interventions depend on the assignment law

the centered conditional value. Since ∂vδ /∂e = δ(m1 − m0 )/Dδ2 , varying the treatment factor
produces the last term. Conditional mean zero and this score identity verify the canonical
gradient in the nonparametric model with finite second moments. This reconstructs Kennedy

were held fixed as P varied. At δ = 1 the expression reduces to Y − E[Y ], as it must: the
target is the observed mean. An arbitrary off-support ma can be used at e = 0 or 1, since its
coefficient vanishes almost surely.
  For δ in a compact subset of (0, ∞), the single-decision likelihood ratio is bounded without
imposing e ∈ [ϵ, 1 − ϵ]. This avoids requesting unsupported actions; it does not make
unsupported fixed-treatment means identifiable. Products of the bounded ratios can still grow
exponentially with the number of decisions. Moreover, the target itself depends on e: correct
outcome regressions alone with an inconsistent propensity do not generally recover it. The
source’s second-order remainders and uniform inference conditions must replace a generic
appeal to double robustness (Kennedy, 2019, Sections 4.3–4.4 and Theorems 3–4).

6.3     Censoring adds an observation intervention
Use Ct = 1 to mean that the trajectory remains observed immediately before action t, with
C0 = 1 and monotone loss thereafter. In this section the clock is Ht , At , Ct+1 , Lt+1 : the next
measurement is recorded only if Ct+1 = 1. Let

                        ct (h, a) = P (Ct+1 = 1 | Ct = 1, Ht = h, At = a).

The full-data outcome exists even if its record is lost. To identify the mean under g and
complete observation, assume consistency, sequential treatment exchangeability, and conditional
independence of retention from the future full-data trajectory given (Ht , At , Ct = 1). Treatment
and retention probabilities must be positive on histories reached by this joint intervention. The
covariate kernels in the g-formula are then estimated among those retained at the corresponding
clock. This is the joint-treatment construction in Hernán and Robins (2020, Section 21.5,
printed pp.275–276).

For a path that is lost, define its summand as zero at its first loss; unobserved later factors are

a newly measured covariate, that covariate must instead precede censoring in the factorization
and enter its conditional model. Using the wrong clock cannot be repaired by increasing model
capacity.
   Recursive augmentation follows by treating action and retention as separate intervention
nodes and applying the longitudinal gradient to the resulting ordered kernels. A combined
weight in an otherwise unmodified regression is not a derivation of the required residuals. The
right-censored setting of Luedtke et al. (2018) develops sequentially doubly robust constructions
for these models. Their conditions concern the appropriate backward nuisance functions, not
arbitrary accuracy on the raw future outcome at every time.
   For servicing, a portfolio transfer can be loss of observation if repayment remains a meaningful
endpoint. If keeping an account on the bank’s platform also changes its service and repayment,
“prevent censoring” has substantive effects. One must specify either an observation-only
monitoring intervention or that actual servicing intervention. Administrative follow-up limits
likewise restrict the identifiable time horizon: weighting cannot reveal events beyond all
customers’ maximum observed duration.

6.5     A fitted observed-history route and its choice against a
        latent model
The longitudinal gradient becomes a practical alternative to a POMDP fit when the recorded
state is a sufficient observed history summary. Consider the three-state servicing process of
Section 58.3, with independent customer trajectories and eight decisions per customer. The
6.5. A fitted observed-history route and its choice against a latent model                               45


state records repayment, arrears or severe distress; repayment is absorbing and has only the
zero action. The policy probabilities are specified before sampling. The two policies’ value
difference is the target, so the covariance between their estimated values must be retained.
   Split whole trajectories into two folds. In the other fold estimate action-specific transition
tables by conditional counts and estimate the behavior probabilities in each eligible state. The
half-count smoothing of sparse cells is fixed in advance. Compute initial Qt , Vt by backward
recursion. On the evaluation fold form the cumulative policy ratios and the discounted-
reward analogue of Equation (5.7). Subtract the two policies’ returns within each customer,
concatenate the folds and use the sample variance of these contrasts divided by the total
number of customers. Treating each customer-date row as independent would discard precisely
the covariance that this score represents.
   For fixed horizon and a finite state/action space with positive occupation probabilities and
overlap on eligible states, table estimates have root-N rates. The second-order longitudinal
remainder is then Op (N −1 ). Cross-fold evaluation and finite-dimensional consistency make the
fitted score difference negligible at root-N scale. The iid trajectory CLT therefore supplies the
stated variance for fixed policies. Deterministic actions in the absorbing state are compatible
with this argument because both evaluation policies take that same action there. The argument
does not cover growing histories or unobserved manager information.

An alternative updates the continuation regression on each evaluation fold while preserving its
allowed financial range. Suppose the discounted remaining reward lies in a known interval
[lt , ut ]. Put qt = (Qt − lt )/(ut − lt ), use its logit as an offset, and fit one intercept ϵt by weighted

Map back to dollars and average the updated Q∗t over the supplied policy to obtain Vt∗ . This

and terminal loss; they are not learned from sample minima and maxima.
   Summing the fitted score equations makes each fold’s mean augmentation term zero up to the
root solver’s tolerance. Thus its targeted plug-in and augmented estimate agree. Evaluation-
fold fitting here is one-dimensional at each of a fixed number of dates, so finite-dimensional
empirical-process control preserves the first-order score expansion. The variance still uses the
full targeted influence values, not just the variance of initial-state predictions. For flexible
evaluation-fold regressions this argument would need replacement; the fact that a targeting
equation was solved is not sufficient by itself.
   In 500 experiments with 3,000 trajectories, changing action probabilities from (0, .2, .4) to
(0, .5, .8) has a true gain of 46.03 per customer. Augmentation and targeting both cover it in
96.8% of runs, with RMSE 4.47 and 4.46. A direct fitted recursion has RMSE 2.87, benefiting
from the correctly specified small transition model, while cumulative weighting has RMSE
4.83. These latter comparisons concern point error; their fitted-model/propensity uncertainty
was not omitted from a purported confidence interval. No interval is reported for them in this
experiment.
46                                                                     Causal analysis for a universal bank


   Changing instead from never assisting to assisting every eligible state has gain 137.24.
Augmentation covers in 95.6% and targeting in 93.6% of runs, with RMSE 29.02 and 24.39.
Direct recursion has RMSE 8.64 and weighting 45.44. The same sample size supports a modest
stochastic change much better than the deterministic policy contrast. All numerical failures
are counted; none occurred in these runs. The 500-replication coverage standard errors are
about one percentage point near 95%.
   The method hierarchy follows the information claim. If recorded history is sufficient, an
augmented or targeted observed-history route avoids latent-state identification assumptions
and allows robust nuisance fitting. A small correct transition model can improve precision, but
its advantage in a simulated Markov population is conditional on that restriction. If recorded
history leaves important hidden state, an identified controlled latent model can add information
through measurement and dynamics, at the cost of their rank, likelihood and assignment
assumptions. In the binary controlled experiment of Section 7.7, 100 randomized replications
give 96% coverage of the 46.31 gain; the Monte Carlo standard error is 0.020. Reducing
emission separation gives 95% coverage over 60 replications, but repayment rewards remain
state-informative, so this is not evidence of uniform performance near singular full-model
information. An omitted private-state logger gives zero coverage and bias −161.26 over 60
replications despite no numerical interval failure. A successful optimizer cannot choose between
these causal information models on the bank’s behalf.

change the customer process, or a model for how it does. It is not the mean among customers
who happened to remain visible.

with small prediction loss can still discard a confounder. Its target concerns decisions based
on observed irregular measurements; a policy based on an unobserved complete trajectory
needs a further measurement model. The source’s mean-aggregation Wald result also does not
automatically extend to its separate robust point aggregators.


6.6.2    Selection, censoring and the fitted comparison

An independent randomized pilot of 2,500 synthetic customers learns a four-coefficient
immediate-reward contrast. The resulting stochastic policy uses action probability .7 where
that fitted contrast exceeds .5 and .2 elsewhere; the reference policy always uses .2. This is
a fixed learned candidate after the pilot, not a proof of dynamic optimality. Conditional on
the pilot, the target is its actual policy value. An unconditional claim about a policy-learning
48                                                                Causal analysis for a universal bank


algorithm would require a different sampling experiment that repeats the pilot as well. Regret
relative to an optimal policy is another estimand.
   Evaluation uses 2,400 fresh customers, four decisions and discount .97. Histories include
a baseline covariate, continuous current and lagged risk, previous action and cumulative
action count. These summaries are sufficient by the declared generator; no generic learned-
state sufficiency is assumed. The action and observation probabilities are fitted with logistic
regressions; arm-specific histogram boosting estimates continuation rewards backward. Two
whole-trajectory folds keep each evaluated customer’s nuisance fits outside that fold. A separate
million-trajectory intervention simulation gives contrast 3.5813 with Monte Carlo standard
error .0040, much smaller than the evaluation interval standard error of about .295.
   Across 120 repetitions under coarsening at random, the full score has bias −.0012, RMSE
.2873 and 95.8% coverage at nominal 95%. Ignoring censoring gives bias −.0199 and 83.3%
coverage: the continuation model is useful, yet its score variance is no longer an adequate
inferential construction. Direct recursion has mean bias −.0376; it is a point challenger without
a claimed interval. In the adverse generator, observation also depends on the otherwise unseen
reward innovation. The full fitted score now has bias −.1434 and 89.2% coverage; ignoring
censoring covers 57.5%. This is an observed failure of the identifying censoring condition, not
proof that a different learner will repair MNAR data. At 120 repetitions the Monte Carlo
standard error of coverage near 95% is about .020.
   Irregular opportunities require a further distinction. One may model the timestamps and
elapsed time as part of each observed history and retain the natural visit clock; changing
when visits occur is a different intervention. The event-intensity likelihood and weights in
Chapter 12 provide that second route. Interpolating missing months and treating them as
observed decisions supplies neither exchangeability nor the visit likelihood. Thus the proposed
servicing workflow first selects among observed-history adjustment, an explicit controlled
measurement model, and a proxy bridge. Their identifying information differs even when all
three output a policy value in the same currency.


6.7     Eligibility changes the population as well as support
Let Et indicate eligibility before action t and require gt (A(Ht ) | Ht ) = 1 for the feasible
action set. An absorbing repaid state can have one action, “no further offer”. Its assignment
is deterministic and causes no positivity defect for policies that also take that action there.
Requesting assistance after repayment is an infeasible intervention, not a rare-treatment
problem.
  An outcome such as satisfaction with an assistance offer may be undefined when no offer is
possible. A policy-specific eligible mean can be expressed as a ratio

eligibility. The always-eligible principal stratum {Etg = Etg = 1} is a cross-world object and is
not recovered by separately estimating these two ratios.
   The eligible treatment effect of Jiang et al. (2025, Section 2.2, equation (1)) holds the prior
treatment path fixed and contrasts the current action among units eligible under that same
prior path. Its no-anticipation, sequential-ignorability and overlap assumptions are stated
on eligible histories; they do not require randomizing eligibility itself. The paper indexes
sequential eligible opportunities with monotone dropout. A bank’s calendar process in which
eligibility disappears and returns needs its own state and event mapping before applying those
formulae.
  These distinctions specify the operations a longitudinal product must accept. An action
policy, a natural-action modification, an observation intervention and an event-removal hypo-
thetical are separate scientific inputs. An interface that records only an outcome column, an
action column and a horizon cannot distinguish their estimands.
Chapter 7

Controlled-state identification,
estimation and customer choice

7.1     What a hidden-state fit must establish
The likelihood and policy-replacement recursions in Chapter 5 leave an identification question
open. Which controlled transition, reward and observation kernels can the recorded law
determine? The answer depends on who sees the state, how actions are assigned, what is
measured, and which actions the target policy will use. A repayment trajectory can identify a
useful predictive state without identifying the effect of an untried restructuring.
   For an uncontrolled stationary K-state HMM, Alexandrovich et al. (2016, Assumptions
A1–A3, Theorem 1) identifies a full-rank ergodic transition matrix and distinct emission
distributions from a block of 2K + 1 observations, up to state-label permutation. Distinct
emissions need not be linearly independent in that theorem. It is a result about the specified
uncontrolled observation law. Treating a privately selected action as an exogenous input
changes its factorization, so the theorem cannot simply be transferred to that fit.
   Identification of the value of one supported policy can require less information than iden-
tification of every state parameter. Conversely, identifying all parameters of one chosen
observational model says nothing about excluded causal models with the same observed law.
The following finite construction separates these issues explicitly.


7.2     A constructive controlled identification result
Let St ∈ {1, . . . , K}, with column vector of probabilities µt , and let Ot ∈ {1, . . . , m}. For
this subsection, the predecision emission matrix E is known from a justified validation model,
Eos = P (Ot = o | St = s). Assume it has full column rank, and let L be a left inverse,
LE = IK . Assume emissions at adjacent dates are independent conditional on their states,
invariant across actions, and measured under the same observation scheme.
   At date t, the action is randomized independently of the state and predecision emission, with
positive probability for each action of interest. Write Ta (s, s′ ) = P (St+1 = s′ | St = s, do(a)),
with row-stochastic Ta , and assume the controlled structural model makes the experiment
identify this kernel. The observable joint matrix conditional on randomized action satisfies

               Ja (o, o′ ) = P (Ot = o, Ot+1 = o′ | At = a) = {E diag(µt )Ta E ′ }oo′ .       (7.1)

The predecision emission distribution gives µt = LpOt . Left- and right-multiplying Equa-

                   Ta = diag(µt )−1 LJa L′ ,    µt (s) > 0 for every recovered row.             (7.2)

This is a constructive sufficient result under known emissions and randomized actions, not an

  For a reward independent of Ot conditional on (St , At ), let ra (s) = E[Rt | St = s, do(a)]

and transition objects. None of the three can be replaced by a good likelihood score.


7.2.1    An observed reward can carry additional state information

Mean rewards suffice for evaluating a policy that ignores reward as information and uses
the recovered signal process. They need not suffice for the full-information belief recursion
in Equation (5.16). If the bank observes the reward before its next decision, its conditional
distribution can change the posterior over states even when its mean is unchanged.
   To identify that richer recursion, strengthen the emission restriction: conditional on
(St , St+1 , At , Rt ) the two signals have independent laws E·St and E·St+1 . For every measurable
reward set D, the observed marked joint matrix then satisfies

           Ja,D (o, o′ ) = P (Ot = o, Rt ∈ D, Ot+1 = o′ | At = a) = E diag(µt )Ka,D E ′ ,

where Ka,D (s, s′ ) = Ta (s, s′ )P (Rt ∈ D | s, a, s′ ). The same multiplication yields

                                     Ka,D = diag(µt )−1 LJa,D L′ .

Thus the marked observed law identifies the transition–reward measure, and division by
Ta (s, s′ ) > 0 identifies its reward conditional law on supported state transitions. For finite
reward categories this is one matrix inversion per category. For general rewards it is an identi-
fication statement about all measurable D, not a finite-sample density-estimation guarantee.
Together with known invariant emissions, these joint kernels supply the information update as
well as expected reward. Merely recovering ra does not establish this stronger result.
   For a summary-preservation counterexample, let a fair binary state persist, with a binary
signal correct with probability 4/5. In one model the first reward is independently +1 or −1
in either state. In the other it is independently +1 or −1 in state zero and +2 or −2 in state
one. Both have the same zero reward mean, transition and signal kernel. At the next decision,
choosing the state correctly pays one. The optimal success probability is 4/5 in the first model
and one in the second, because absolute reward reveals the state. Their full reward observation
laws differ; the example proves insufficiency of the compressed mean-reward interface, not
nonidentification from the full marked law.
  For an exact two-state example take
                         !                !                          !                      !
              4/5 1/5                 3/5               4/5 1/5                  3/5 2/5
        E=            ,        µ=         ,    T0 =              ,       T1 =             .
              1/5 4/5                 2/5              3/10 7/10                1/10 9/10

Computing J0 , J1 and applying the inverse recovers both transitions exactly. If the two columns
of E instead coincide, observations cannot distinguish the states through this construction.
If the columns become nearly equal, L becomes large and finite-sample errors are amplified

twice in LJa L′ . A fitted state dimension that exceeds the measurement rank can therefore be
computationally feasible and scientifically unsupported.
  For a logger using only the private state, the analogous joint matrix is E diag{µt (s)q(a |
s)}Ta E ′ before normalization. That selection factor cannot be ignored. Extra observed proxies,
a validated logging model or interventions can identify it under additional restrictions; the
action-conditioned matrix alone is not the randomized matrix above.


7.3     Proxy value identification without a complete latent fit
Past and current observations can sometimes serve as two views of the hidden state. The
matrix identification result of Tennenholtz et al. (2020, Section 3, Theorem 1) uses specific
invertibility conditions and the declared behavior/evaluation information sets. An independent
hidden state at every date can destroy the needed past-to-current rank: a long history is then
not automatically an informative proxy for today’s private confounder.
   The bridge approach makes the connection to Chapter 4 more explicit. Bennett and Kallus
(2023, Section 4, Assumptions 1–2 and Theorem 2) uses a hybrid law Pt∗ that applies the target
policy before t and the logging policy from t onward. For a deterministic target, let Dt be the
action that its observed information would select. Its negative-control restriction has the form

                            (Zt , At ) ⊥ (Wt , Dt , Yt (a)) | Ut   under Pt∗ ,

for the allowed future outcome variables Yt . Here Zt is the action-side proxy, Wt the outcome-
side proxy and Ut the sufficient hidden confounder, possibly augmented by observed context.
This is stronger than saying both proxies predict repayment. In particular, giving the target
policy extra history can invalidate independence of Zt and Dt , even if the physical environment
is unchanged.
   The source’s Assumption 2 requires existence of latent action and outcome bridges qt† , h†t
satisfying

                  E∗t [qt† (Zt , At ) | Ut , At = a] = Pt∗ (At = a | Ut )−1 ,
                 E∗t [h†t (Wt , At ) | Ut , At = a] = E∗t [1(Dt = At )Yt | Ut , At = a].

This includes latent action positivity. It is stronger than merely finding solutions of observed
conditional equations, and is separate from the negative-control independence. Under these
two assumptions its Theorem 2 allows solutions qt , ht of the corresponding observable equations

                  E∗t [qt (Zt , At ) | Wt , At = a] = Pt∗ (At = a | Wt )−1 ,
                 E∗t [ht (Wt , At ) | Zt , At = a] = E∗t [1(Dt = At )Yt | Zt , At = a].

The outcome on the right is recursively constructed from later bridges. These observed
solutions need not be asserted to be the latent bridges themselves. The theorem uses latent
existence and the independence restriction to justify the causal target of the observed solution.
The static augmented-bridge cancellation can then be applied at each hybrid-law step. The
resulting observed-trajectory functional identifies policy value without assigning a uniquely
interpretable latent state to each account. Bridge existence, support and estimation stability
remain necessary; the identification result is not a claim that every matrix inverse or neural
minimax fit will be reliable.
   In the source’s tabular example with Ut = St , Zt = Ot−1 , Wt = Ot and a policy using only
Ot , the outcome bridge requires solving a linear system through Et′ = P (Ot | St )′ . The action
bridge additionally involves the backward state kernel Pt∗ (St−1 | St ) (Bennett and Kallus,
7.4. Estimating a controlled likelihood                                                         53


2023, Proposition 1). Full ranks provide a sufficient solvability route, but the backward kernel
depends on the induced policy law. It must be checked for that law; invertibility of each
action-specific transition should not be substituted for checking a policy-dependent mixture
without proof. For example, I2 and the two-state swap matrix are both invertible, whereas
their equal mixture has rank one. This is the same distinction between structural identification
and inverse stability encountered in NPIV, now at each decision date.


7.4     Estimating a controlled likelihood
For finite states, let Kt (s, s′ ) collect the action, transition, reward and next-emission factors
of Equation (5.14). The forward recursion multiplies a row distribution by Kt , normalizes
                                                   P
by ct , and accumulates log L = log cinitial + t log ct . Scaling at each step avoids numerical
underflow. A backward recursion gives smoothed state probabilities γt (s) and adjacent-state
probabilities ξt (s, s′ ).
   An EM update maximizes the conditional expectation of the complete log likelihood. When
parameters separate and transitions are unrestricted row probabilities, its action-specific
transition update is                  P                        ′
                                  ′     i,t 1(Ait = a)ξit (s, s )
                          Ta (s, s ) = P
                           b                                      .                    (7.3)
                                          i,t 1(Ait = a)γit (s)

Emission, reward and logger updates maximize their own expected log factors when that
factorization is valid. The sufficient counts generalize the HMM forward–backward construction
of Rabiner (1989). If the logger uses private state, omitting its likelihood factor changes γ, ξ
and therefore every update, even if actions themselves have no parameters of interest.
   The usual likelihood ascent follows by Jensen’s inequality applied to the latent posterior at
the old parameter: increasing its expected complete log likelihood increases a lower bound
tight at the old parameter. Exact ascent does not guarantee the global maximum, a correct
number of states or causal identification. Multiple starts, held-out predictive checks, nearly
empty states, rank diagnostics, boundary transitions and sensitivity to priors or penalties are
material to interpreting a fit. Bayesian estimation instead averages over a parameter posterior
proportional to L(θ, η)p(θ, η); it does not turn a likelihood equivalence into data identification.


7.4.1    Continuous states and numerical alternatives

For a linear Gaussian model with known/exogenous input,

                      St+1 = F St + Bat + ηt+1 ,      Ot+1 = CSt+1 + νt+1 ,

Gaussian conditioning gives predictive mean m− = F mt + Bat , covariance P − = F Pt F ′ + Q,
innovation covariance V = CP − C ′ + R, gain K = P − C ′ V −1 , and

                   mt+1 = m− + K(Ot+1 − Cm− ),           Pt+1 = P − − KV K ′ .

The innovation density also supplies the likelihood increment. This is the conditional-Gaussian
derivation of Särkkä (2013, Theorem 4.2 and Theorem 12.1) with a deterministic input added.
State-dependent observation selection or a privately chosen discrete action can make the
conditional state law non-Gaussian, even when the transition and emission equations are linear.
  Nonlinear Gaussian filters approximate moments through linearization, sigma points or
quadrature. Particle methods approximate distributions using weighted samples; variational
methods optimize within a restricted distribution family. These approximations have different
54                                                                      Causal analysis for a universal bank


failure modes. A small covariance from a Gaussian approximation can miss a second mode; a
particle cloud can lose a low-probability state that matters for a rare default; a variational
objective can be accurate for its loss and inaccurate for policy tail risk.
  For sequential importance sampling, a particle transition proposal q prop (s′ | s, new data)
requires the incremental weight

                            qη (at | s, Ht )Tat (s, s′ )F (rt | s, at , s′ )B(ot+1 | s′ , at )
                wt+1 ∝ wt                                                                      .
                                             q prop (s′ | s, new data)

It is the target/proposal path-density ratio (Särkkä, 2013, Section 7.3), with the private logger
retained. For a known observed-history action probability, its factor is constant across state
particles and cancels in normalized filtering weights. Under intervention it is replaced by the
specified policy. State weights, parameter uncertainty and policy uncertainty are separate
objects. Resampling effective sample size is a useful weight diagnostic, not a bound on the
error of a default-probability estimate.


7.5     Errors in the model and errors in numerical solution
An explicit bound helps decide where computational precision matters. For a fixed Markov
policy on a common finite state space, v = r + γP v with 0 < γ < 1. For an alternative (re, Pe ),
suppose ∥r − re∥∞ ≤ ϵr , sups ∥P (s, ·) − Pe (s, ·)∥1 ≤ ϵP and both rewards have magnitude at
most R. Subtract the two Bellman equations and use ∥ve∥∞ ≤ R/(1 − γ):

                                                    ϵr   γRϵP
                                 ∥v − ve∥∞ ≤           +         .                                     (7.4)
                                                  1 − γ (1 − γ)2

An initial-distribution error contributes at most R∥µ − µe∥1 /(1 − γ). This project bound
assumes that the compared kernels represent the same causal state/action system. It cannot
align two causally nonidentified models by fiat. A POMDP extension needs a valid comparison
of its induced belief processes and information sets.
   For a contraction T , an approximate value vb with Bellman residual at most ϵB satisfies
∥vb − v∥∞ ≤ ϵB /(1 − γ): insert T vb between vb and T v and rearrange. Numerical tolerance can
therefore be chosen in the units of the decision value. It should be smaller than the material
statistical and model uncertainty, but its smallness establishes neither of them.
   Dense forward/backward fitting costs O(N T K 2 ) for N independent trajectories; declared
sparse transitions can reduce the per-step matrix cost. Trajectories can be partitioned and
sufficient expected counts combined. A long single series still carries temporal dependence, and
state sparsity is a model restriction if imposed for speed. Numerical adapters should report
the likelihood approximation, rank, solver tolerances and resource measurements separately
from causal qualification.


7.6     Unknown emissions: identification for the model actually
        fitted
A known measurement matrix is a valuable baseline, but it does not justify estimating that
matrix from the same unvalidated records. A small controlled model permits a constructive
extension. Consider two states and two signals, an unknown invertible emission matrix E with
columns summing to one, unknown row-stochastic transitions Ta , and an unknown positive
initial law µ0 . Require one invertible baseline transition T0 . Across independent trajectories,

actions are assigned independently of states, signals and previous innovations, with positive
probabilities. Signal draws are conditionally independent given their states and invariant across
actions. Conditional on the current state/action, a binary repayment reward is independent
of signal and next-state draws. These restrictions describe one initial supported POMDP
estimation experiment; they are not assumptions learned from EM convergence.
  Condition on A0 = A1 = 0. Independent assignment makes this the observation law under
two imposed baseline actions. Conditional on S1 , the three signals O0 , O1 , O2 are independent.

   This proof is a project construction using three observed views. Azizzadenesheli et al. (2016,
Sections 3.1–3.2) develops a broader controlled spectral route with action-conditioned views,
rank assumptions, a memoryless logging policy and single-trajectory mixing bounds. Its small
singular values enter the finite-sample requirements explicitly. That is the relevant comparison
to an uncontrolled HMM theorem: the action’s dependence on observations changes the views.
Augmenting the state by the action and asserting generic HMM full rank can instead introduce
a rank-deficient transition matrix.
   Three limitations follow from the proof itself. An almost singular E, T0 or P02 amplifies
sampling error; identification is not a conditioning guarantee. With more hidden states than
signal categories, this two-view inversion fails, even though a different multi-period theorem
may apply. Finally, conditioning on baseline actions chosen using private information need not
leave the experimental law used in the first line. A logger-specific joint model or additional
experimental/proxy information is then necessary. Under the special private-state-only logger,
known emissions can sometimes recover µ(s)q(a | s) from the joint matrix and recover Ta
by row normalization. Failure of the naive conditional likelihood is therefore not a universal
impossibility theorem for every private-logger model.

7.7.1    The regular sampling argument and its failures

Take N independent complete trajectories and fixed H. Suppose the true probabilities are in
the interior of the declared compact box, rank and emission separation hold, labels are fixed,
and the information matrix I = E[si s′i ] = −E[∂ϑ si ] is nonsingular. For finite alphabets there
are finitely many observed trajectory patterns. Their empirical frequencies obey a uniform law
of large numbers; positivity bounds the pattern log likelihoods and derivatives. The expected
log likelihood is uniquely maximized at the identified law by nonnegativity of Kullback–Leibler
divergence. A global approximate maximizer is therefore consistent on the label-ordered
compact parameter space. Taylor expansion of its score yields

an argument for the actual sampling law, not a generic claim about a single dependent series
or growing H. Multiple EM starts do not prove global maximization. Boundary solutions,
singular information, optimizer caps and disagreement between starts must remain reported
failures or conditional fits.
  For a policy π fixed before evaluation, let Vπ (ϑ) be the expected discounted recorded financial
reward. For finite alphabets and fixed horizon, summing over hidden paths and observed

7.7.2    Numerical tolerance in the same units as policy value

Within a basin where the negative average log-likelihood Hessian has smallest eigenvalue at least
κ > 0, an average score residual ϵs bounds parameter optimization error by ϵs /κ. A gradient
bound ∥∇V ∥ ≤ GV then gives value error at most GV ϵs /κ. For asymptotic equivalence in
Equation (7.7), require ϵs = o(N −1/2 ) as well as selection of the correct basin. The observed
eigenvalue is a local diagnostic, not proof of a uniform population curvature bound. Solver
success and small likelihood increments alone do not establish an acceptable monetary error.
   Spectral moment inversion is a meaningful alternative: it has a constructive population
solution and avoids iterative latent-path fitting, but inverses and eigengaps can amplify noisy
empirical moments into negative probabilities. Constrained likelihood uses all recorded patterns
and enforces valid probabilities at a cost in nonconvex optimization. Spectral initialization,
likelihood refinement and the exact small-state reference therefore serve different purposes.
Gaussian filtering, particle likelihood and variational inference retain the approximation
distinctions in the preceding section; none inherits this finite-alphabet likelihood theorem
without a new argument.


7.8     A value-error bound on the actual partially observed pro-
        cess
The fully observed bound in Equation (7.4) does not by itself compare two belief processes. A
path-law argument does. Align the same latent labels and observed alphabet in two controlled
models. Let the initial joint state/signal laws differ by at most δ0 in L1 . Let the joint one-step
kernel for reward, next state and next signal, given current state and action, differ by at most
δK uniformly. Use the same policy kernel on every observed history in both models. Its state
in this argument is the complete history together with the latent state, not just the current
observed signal.

   Markov kernels contract L1 distance. Insert the first model’s one-step kernel between the
two propagated path laws and apply the triangle inequality. Induction bounds the path-law
distance through reward t by δ0 + (t + 1)δK . If |Rt | ≤ R, integration gives

respects partial observation and policy information. Comparing different optimal policies or

7.9       Private decisions and independently validated measure-
          ments
An arrears officer may see information absent from the warehouse. Adding states to a predictive
HMM does not explain that information. A tractable alternative obtains an independent
labelled measurement sample and models the action mechanism explicitly. Let St have K
states, Ot have M signal categories, and At have two actions. On one decision clock assume
                                                                             2
     Ot | St ∼ E·St ,     At | St ∼ qSt ,       Rt | St , At ∼ N (rAt ,St , σR ),      St+1 | St , At ∼ TAt (St , ·).

The displayed factors assert conditional independence of signal, logger randomness and
reward noise given the indicated parents. Reward occurs before the next signal. Conditional
independence, time invariance, state labels and the action/transition modularity are scientific
premises. The validation sample observes labelled (S, O) under the same emission law; labels
sampled uniformly across states need not reproduce the population state frequencies. Their
conditional emission likelihood is the relevant contribution.

7.9.3      Numerical and inferential challengers

The new finite experiment fits three states, four signals, private logging, eight decisions, 600
customer trajectories and either 90 or 600 validation labels. It estimates 32 parameters using
two data-based starts. Reward noise standard deviation is known at 12. The true fixed
observable-policy contrast is 59.5645. With 90 labels, bias is 2.0798 and coverage .850; with
600, bias is .1926 and coverage .875. These denominators include all 80 requested replications
per case, including four and five boundary/numerical failures. Those failures yield unavailable
inference. Model, sandwich and fixed-emission approximations happen to give the same
coverage here; the reward is informative about state and the measured calibration contribution
is small. This experiment does not demonstrate a large calibration variance penalty. Omitting
the private logger on the first 20 datasets yields biases of −36.51 and −41.12, respectively.
   The first 600-label dataset was selected before a 199-refit parametric bootstrap challenger. It
resimulates complete trajectories and independent emission measurements conditional on the
audited label counts, then refits the complete model. Seventeen refits hit a boundary or failed,
exceeding the prespecified 5% availability limit, so no percentile/basic interval is released. The
standard deviation among 182 usable refits is 10.20, only a descriptive conditional diagnostic.
Extra starts change the fitted contrast by .0012 and the average negative log likelihood by less
than 10−10 . Information differencing steps 3 × 10−5 , 10−4 , 3 × 10−4 change the model standard
error by less than 4 × 10−8 . The local information condition number is about 1,929. These
checks make numerical roundoff an implausible sole explanation of the observed undercoverage;
they do not prove the global optimum or finite-sample normality.
   The method decision is therefore explicit: this validated finite route is an identified research
fit with a useful value functional, but its current normal/bootstrapped interval is not a
routine calibrated product default. The larger-sample and audited-trajectory experiments in
Section 7.13 provide selected alternatives; they do not retroactively qualify this 600-trajectory
interval. Weak-state/profile inference and bank measurement validation remain distinct
requirements. The observed failure is part of the proposal’s method hierarchy, not a hidden
exception.


7.9.4      Proxies identify a different object with different information

Sequential proxy bridges can identify value without recovering a uniquely labelled latent
transition model (Bennett and Kallus, 2023; Zhang and Tchetgen Tchetgen, 2024). Their
conditional independence and completeness restrictions are different from labelled measurement
validation. The two-stage dynamic-regime source identifies joint counterfactual quantities
along compatible treatment histories under its stated bridge restrictions; it does not identify
every cross-world joint law. Bridge existence must be asserted or proved separately from
uniqueness. For an operator K, injectivity means Kh = 0 implies h = 0; it does not mean
that every observed right-hand side lies in range(K).
   This matters for missing rewards. The 2026 missingness-aware MDP preprint uses augmented
state, a shadow next-state variable, exclusion and completeness to motivate a bridge (Wei
et al., 2026, Assumptions 3.1–3.4, Theorem 3.6). Its general existence discussion cannot be
adopted from injectivity alone. For the product’s operator contract require an integrable
7.10. An exactly Gaussian controlled model with private logging                                          61


bridge solution and the relevant range condition, then uniqueness/identification and an inverse-
problem regularization analysis. In a finite square full-rank system existence follows for every
right-hand side; an infinite-dimensional conditional expectation operator needs more. Overlap,
residual and rank diagnostics are conditional checks. They cannot certify the unobserved
exclusion and completeness assumptions that make an MNAR query causal.


7.10       An exactly Gaussian controlled model with private logging
The finite-state construction leaves a numerical question: can a controlled continuous-state
likelihood retain the private action mechanism and still admit exact filtering and derivatives? A
scalar Gaussian reference supplies an affirmative answer under specific measurement restrictions.
Let

       X0 ∼ N (0, 1),                      Ot = Xt + νt ,                   At = kXt + ηt ,          (7.10)
       Rt = cXt + dAt + ϵt ,            Xt+1 = f Xt + bAt + ωt+1 .                                   (7.11)

All primitive noises are independent with known positive variances (ro , ra , rr , q). The unknown
coefficients are (f, b, k, c, d). The signal loading is calibrated to one and the initial law fixes
the state scale. Actions are continuous here, such as a scaled assistance amount. Known
noise variances and invariant measurements are a substantial price for this exact reference, not
defaults for arbitrary bank feeds.

preferred extension for poorly conditioned systems.

Gaussian density. This agrees with the sequential likelihood; central differences independently
check the analytic score. These checks include the action channel and reward transform, not
only a Kalman recursion with fixed inputs. They meet the numerical obligation to differentiate
the likelihood being optimized.

The historical coefficient k disappears from the intervention law. Policy signal noise affects
the distribution even though its mean is zero; the displayed recursion is sufficient for a linear
expected reward, not a default-tail probability or nonlinear utility. Every prescribed action lies
in the historical Gaussian law’s topological support. Nevertheless the deterministic conditional
policy is singular relative to its continuous logging density, so ordinary importance weighting
does not apply. This identification rests on the structural functional form and identified
coefficients, not a bounded-density-ratio theorem. A finite horizon needs no infinite-horizon
stability; an infinite value would need appropriate growth/discount conditions.
   The experiment uses H = 12, N = 800, coefficients (.6, .35, .8, 1.4, −.2) and noise variances
(q, ro , ra , rr ) = (.3, .4, .5, .7). The policy has (α, β, γ) = (.4, −.2, .97), giving true value 2.6785
relative to the zero-action, zero-mean reward reference. Across 160 repetitions the joint
Gaussian fit has bias −.0020 and nominal 95% coverage .9625, with no unusable fit. The Monte
Carlo standard error near this coverage is .015. The exogenous-input challenger omitting
private logging has value bias .9531. Only a point comparison is made for that misspecified
likelihood. The initial likelihood and gradient identity checks are retained with the experiment,
as are optimizer residuals and information conditioning.
  This comparison supplies a selected continuous route, not a blanket POMDP estimator.
For discrete private actions with a logistic state-dependent logger, the posterior is generally
non-Gaussian; the exact recursion above no longer applies. An extended/unscented filter
approximates moments and may bias likelihood derivatives. Quadrature is a deterministic
7.11. Customer choice is an inverse decision problem                                             63


challenger in low dimension, requiring node/tolerance sensitivity. Particle likelihood keeps
the logger in the weights, with independent particle replicates and particle-number studies
separating Monte Carlo variation from parameter sampling uncertainty. Differentiating a
resampling implementation requires its own argument; a formal derivative of smooth transition
densities is not automatically the derivative of the stochastic objective actually used.
   For a locally strongly curved average negative log likelihood with Hessian lower bound κ,
an average score error εs moves the local solution by at most approximately εs /κ. A value-
gradient bound G then contributes Gεs /κ to numerical value error. Likelihood approximation
adds its own score error, and value quadrature or simulation adds a separate term. This
conditional error budget explains why reducing solver tolerance cannot repair measurement
misspecification. The exact Gaussian route is a reusable benchmark for numerical adapters;
richer state models require renewed identification, derivative and uncertainty qualification.


7.11      Customer choice is an inverse decision problem
The bank can optimize a supplied reward while a customer chooses whether to refinance,
accept an offer or default. Estimating that customer’s behavior reverses the direction of the
decision problem: choices and transitions are observed, and preferences are unknown. Let x
be the customer’s observed Markov state, d a customer action, ud (x) its flow utility, and Pd
its transition matrix. Assume independent choice shocks with a specified type-I extreme-value
law, normalized so that the expected maximum has no additive constant, and a specified
discount 0 ≤ β < 1. Then

                      vd (x) = ud (x) + β(Pd V )(x),
                                    X                            exp vd (x)
                      V (x) = log       exp vd (x),    pd (x) = P             .              (7.17)
                                    d                            j exp vj (x)

The log odds identify vd −v0 = log(pd /p0 ) under this model, not the flow-utility difference alone.
Future transitions enter the choice-specific values. The conditional independence restriction
on next-period states and shocks, information available to customers, discount and shock
normalization are structural assumptions (Kalouptsidi et al., 2021, Section 2).
  Using v0 = V + log p0 gives

                        V = (I − βP0 )−1 (u0 − log p0 ),
                       ud = (I − βPd )(I − βP0 )−1 (u0 − log p0 ) + log pd .                 (7.18)

The inverse exists because the Neumann series k≥0 β k P0k converges. Thus observed CCPs

and transitions leave the vector u0 free unless further restrictions identify it. Equation (7.18)
reconstructs the reference-payoff argument in equations (3)–(5) of the cited paper. A constant
utility location and scale are familiar normalizations; fixing an entire state-dependent payoff
vector is more consequential.


7.11.1    The same choices can imply different policy responses

For any bounded state function c, define

                              ucd = ud + c − βPd c,        V c = V + c.                      (7.19)

Then vdc = vd + c for every action at that state, so all choice probabilities are unchanged. This
is a constructive observational equivalence, with a telescoping discounted reward interpretation.
64                                                               Causal analysis for a universal bank


If a counterfactual changes Pd while retaining the two candidate flow-utility models, the
cancellation need not persist. It is precisely the requested counterfactual that must be
identified, rather than every payoff or merely the historical choice probabilities (Kalouptsidi
et al., 2021).
   In a two-state example, let β = 1/2, both historical action transitions equal I, and all
baseline utilities equal zero. Customers choose each action with probability 1/2. Taking
c = (0, 2)′ gives equivalent utilities ucd = (0, 1)′ for both actions. Now let action 1 move
either state to state 1 while action 0 preserves the state. The zero-utility model still predicts
probability 1/2 of action 1. In the second model, state 1 has V1 = 2(1 + log 2) and, writing
z = exp(V0 /2), z 2 = z + 2e. Thus
                                                          √

                                           z                2
which exceeds 1/2. Both models fit the same historical choices and transitions. The new
transition makes their policy predictions differ. In mortgage applications, a modification that
changes repayment/default transitions needs more identification than a well-fitted historical
refinancing-choice likelihood.


7.12      Estimation alternatives and the bank–customer interface
A full-solution likelihood estimates utility/transition parameters and solves Equation (7.17) at
each parameter value. A CCP route estimates choice probabilities and transitions first, then
uses an inversion such as Equation (7.18) with identifying restrictions on payoffs. It trades
repeated dynamic programming for first-stage approximation and support requirements: very
small CCPs make log odds unstable, and unobserved customer types cannot be ignored by
pooling their nonlinear choice probabilities.
   Bayesian estimation can integrate preference uncertainty, but the likelihood still depends on
a value solution. Imai et al. (2009, Sections 2.2–2.3) compares conventional nested posterior
simulation with an algorithm that coordinates parameter simulation and approximate value
updates. Its convergence result has explicit regularity, compactness, memory and bandwidth
conditions (Assumptions 1–8 and Theorems 1–2). Performing one approximate Bellman update
inside arbitrary MCMC does not inherit that result.
   For the normalized logit model, a value error at most ϵV changes each vd by at most βϵV .
Since log-sum-exp is one-Lipschitz in sup norm, each log choice probability changes by at
most 2βϵV . Combined with the Bellman-residual bound, this gives a transparent likelihood
error budget. It is a deterministic approximation bound, not a sampling theorem for the fitted
preferences.
   The bank’s action a should remain distinct from the customer’s response d. An offer can
change a contractual cost in ud (x; a), the transition law Pd (· | x; a), or the information available
to the customer. A structural intervention must state which mechanism changes and what
remains invariant. Competitor repricing, funding conditions and capacity can then alter the
environment again. A single-customer policy response conditional on those quantities is not
automatically a banking-group equilibrium effect. The product must return the corresponding
target and require an explicit equilibrium model for the latter question.
7.13. A resolved information and inference design for servicing                                  65


7.13      A resolved information and inference design for servicing
The privately logged three-state model is useful precisely because it can fail despite an identified
population value. Resolving that failure requires separating the statistical experiment from
the optimizer and from the proposed decision. Here the servicing decision is whether to offer
temporary assistance; the objective is discounted collected cash net of assistance and operating
cost. Signals arrive before the decision, while the cash rewards used in this four-decision policy
are settled after its decision horizon. The policy may use signals and its own previous actions.
It may not use the later audited state or settled cash as contemporaneous information.


7.13.1    What the retained failure actually shows

For the original 600-trajectory experiment, all nine unavailable fits were on a constrained
transition-logit boundary. Reconstructing those exact seeds reproduces the stored values,
rather than diagnosing a different simulation. With 90 emission labels, 76 of 80 fits were
available: conditional coverage was .8947, empirical value standard deviation 10.668 and mean
model standard error 9.657. With 600 labels, 75 were available: conditional coverage was .9333,
empirical standard deviation 9.141 and mean standard error 9.687. Counting unavailable fits
gives the previously reported .850 and .875. The latter case therefore does not mainly show
underestimated standard errors among the usable fits. Availability, tail error and bias are
different questions. Eighty repetitions leave substantial Monte Carlo uncertainty.
   The binding coordinates are transition logits, including near-zero destinations under privately
selected actions. Larger emission calibration alone does not supply those scarce action/state
transitions. The model’s positive population transition probabilities do not prevent an observed
likelihood maximum near the boundary. The observed fit reconstructions, larger-trajectory
follow-up and complete-state frequency experiment separate this scarcity explanation from
the earlier differencing/start checks. They do not certify a global maximum or establish one
universal cause of undercoverage. At 3,000 observational trajectories and 600 independent
emission labels, all 120 follow-up fits are available; coverage is .9417, bias −.213, empirical
standard deviation 4.097 and mean reported standard error 4.301. This supports a bounded
larger-sample regime on this mechanism, not a universal 3,000-customer rule. The failed
199-refit bootstrap remains adverse evidence for the original design.


7.13.2    A measurement acquisition alternative

An independent representative audit now follows whole customer trajectories, recording the
state before each action, the same production signal, the actual action and the eventually
settled reward. The states must have an operational definition: for example, a predecision
classification of verified repayment capacity and available liquidity into solvent, temporarily
constrained and persistent-shortfall categories. Definition and thresholds are fixed before
outcomes. Independent adjudication checks timestamped income, obligations and accessible
balances; disagreements and unavailable documents remain measurement failures.
   These categories are not automatically sufficient causal states. The model asserts that, condi-
tional on the state, the officer’s private action information adds no further outcome/transition
cause; that the state is Markov for this horizon; and that the audit and production emissions
agree. A coarse affordability label can violate all three. Audit selection must represent the
target population, or known inclusion probabilities and their influence must enter the estimator.
The implementation below assumes representative independent trajectories. It does not silently
replace a convenience audit by a random sample.

The finite recursion is the belief-state planning construction (Kaelbling et al., 1998). Four
signals, two actions and four decisions permit exact tree enumeration here. The tree is optimized
using an independent 2,000-trajectory audit pilot, then frozen in its entirety. Evaluation fits
kernels on separate audited trajectories and propagates their uncertainty through this fixed
tree. It differentiates neither the argmax nor the pilot training procedure. The interval targets
the value of the policy that was actually trained, conditional on that pilot, not the unknown
optimal value.
   To evaluate the fixed tree without numerical posterior divisions, propagate unnormalized
state mass. At each signal branch multiply by E·o , add the selected action’s expected reward,
and propagate through Ta . Summing all leaves gives a polynomial in the kernels and initial
law, linear in the rewards. Its derivative is therefore well-defined for the fixed tree; central
differencing is checked against a smaller step and independent likelihood/count perturbations.
Exact enumeration avoids a filter approximation error in this selected problem. Larger horizons
require pruning or approximate planning and an explicit value-loss bound.
7.13. A resolved information and inference design for servicing                                67


   On the common mechanism the frozen learned policy has true four-period contrast 25.029
against never assisting. Some actions depend on earlier signals even after holding the current
signal and remaining horizon fixed; this is a belief-history policy, rather than an immediate-
reward rule. At 1,200 audited evaluation trajectories, all 400 fits are available and coverage
is .950 for this contrast. The original eight-period fixed-signal contrast has coverage .9425.
At 300 audited paths, 54 of 400 fits have an empty category; all-request coverage is .8275 for
the learned policy even though coverage conditional on availability is .9566. Measurement-
supported identification therefore still requires enough informative visits.


7.13.4    Three information routes on the same servicing problem

An observed-history g-formula substitutes the factual conditional law given public signals and
actions. Under private logging its state posterior after action a is proportional to bo (s)qs (a),
while the intervention posterior is bo (s). Thus even an exactly estimated public-history
conditional law uses the wrong state mixture for the intervention. Adding a flexible learner
cannot remove this information gap. Recording the action-relevant private information,
or randomizing assistance with adequate support, changes that conclusion. The common-
mechanism comparison evaluates both recursions on the same frozen policy. Its exact public-
history g-formula contrast is −35.647, against the intervention contrast 25.029. The sign
reversal occurs even without nuisance estimation error.
   Validated emissions can identify the kernels using the earlier marked moment/hidden-
likelihood route, with fewer labels but difficult finite curvature and boundary behavior. Fully
audited trajectories identify the same kernels and policy target more directly, with the explicit
acquisition cost above. Their precision and availability are properties of different sampling
designs, not proof that hidden-state modeling is unnecessary.
   Proximal evaluation instead seeks policy value without recovering named states. For this
servicing mechanism an action-side proxy might be a separately recorded officer assessment, and
an outcome-side proxy an independent affordability measurement. Merely calling them proxies
proves nothing: after conditioning on the latent confounder and allowed context, the action-side
proxy and logged action must be independent of the outcome-side proxy, proposed action and
counterfactual continuation under the source’s hybrid laws. The proposed policy cannot reuse
forbidden private proxy information. Bennett and Kallus (2023, Assumptions 1–2, Theorem 2
and Table 1) give these policy-dependent restrictions and the recursive action/outcome bridges.
In particular their outcome bridge targets E[1{Et = At }Yt | Ut , At = a], where Et denotes the
proposed action; dropping that indicator changes the theorem.
  The source’s recursive bridge score is a substantive challenger when the bank can defend
those exclusions and bridge existence/rank conditions but cannot obtain accurate state labels.
The current production feed has one public signal stream and no independently validated second
proxy. It cannot invoke that theorem by relabelling the same signal twice. If an additional
proxy is collected, its conditional operator, range, regularization and policy information set
become new scientific inputs. This explains why the audited trajectory route is selected for the
bounded decision capability and proximal evaluation remains a qualified alternative, rather
than claiming that one existing dataset satisfies all three information regimes.


7.13.5    The initial product boundary

The offering includes finite-state estimation and observable-history policy evaluation under
a qualified measurement design, plus the earlier exact linear-Gaussian controlled likelihood.
It does not include arbitrary nonlinear private-state fitting with routinely calibrated policy
68                                                                                    Causal analysis for a universal bank


intervals. Choosing an extended Kalman or particle filter would require a declared likelihood,
initial/noise laws, derivative accuracy and policy-value comparison against a numerical reference,
following the approximation obligations already derived. Section 7.14 supplies a selected
audited nonlinear comparison with additional information and policy-class restrictions. Those
restrictions affect which bank requests can be accepted; they are not postponed as a generic
deployment check. A noisy or selected audit also changes the statistical model, even when
all matrices are well-conditioned. In a separately registered 200-repetition sensitivity run,
independently misclassifying 10% of predecision state labels at 1,200 audit trajectories produces
bias −105.72 for the original 59.56 contrast and zero coverage. This is a specific severe
misspecification example, not a calibrated bound for every 10% audit-error process.


7.14      An audited nonlinear servicing experiment
The exact Gaussian construction leaves a substantive question: what changes when the state
transition bends and a private binary decision reveals hidden state information? A small
servicing experiment gives a complete answer for one identified model. It also exposes the
difference between an accurate likelihood and a reliable routine interval.
  For each independent customer the order is state, signal, action, reward, then next state. In
units fixed by an accurate state audit, let

                             S0 ∼ N (µ0 , v0 ),                                                   Ot = St + et ,        (7.21)
                           St+1 = ρSt + γ tanh(St ) + βAt + ut+1 ,
      Pr(At = 1 | St , Ot ) = ϵ + (1 − 2ϵ) expit(λ0 + λs St + λo Ot ),
                            Rt = η0 + ηs St + ηa At + ηsa St At + vtR .                                                 (7.22)

Independent Gaussian innovations have positive variances q, ro , rR . Their log variances, both
initial parameters, three transition coefficients, three logger coefficients and four reward
coefficients give 15 unknowns. The fixed logger floor is ϵ = .05; stability requires |ρ| + |γ| < 1.
Rewards are in thousands of currency units. These are synthetic scientific restrictions, not a
fitted description of a real bank.


7.14.1      Identification comes from the observation design

Production observes (O, A, R); an independent representative audit observes complete labelled
(S, O, A, R) trajectories. The loading one in O = S + e and the labelled scale of S fix state
meaning. Under positive definite population Gram matrices, regressing St+1 on (St , tanh St , At )
identifies the three transition coefficients and its residual identifies q. The signal residual
identifies ro . Regressing reward on (1, St , At , St At ) identifies its coefficients and variance;
labelled initial states identify (µ0 , v0 ). The clipped logistic probability is strictly increasing in
its index. Equality of these probabilities on a full-rank support for (1, S, O) therefore implies
equality of the logger coefficients. The positive action floor supports both actions; full rank
and representative labels remain substantive requirements. This establishes identification
before filtering. Filtering does not create the audited states. Noisy or selected labels change
this argument.

information. Retaining a state-dependent logistic logger would invalidate the reduction. The
bootstrap particle challenger instead keeps the private logger in its weights. Eight independent
seeds at 512 and 4,096 particles expose Monte Carlo variation. Coupled finite differences assess
stochastic likelihood perturbations; they are not a certified derivative through a discontinuous
resampling path. These are substantive alternatives to Gaussian projection, as emphasized by
Särkkä (2013, Chapters 6–7).
