before any stated finite-cluster correction. The reduction key is the statistical cluster, not
the worker partition. With score values (1, 1, −1, −1) in two clusters (1, 1) and (−1, −1), the
cluster meat is 8; treating rows as independent gives 4. Sharding each cluster across workers
and squaring partial sums before regrouping repeats that error. Correct distributed execution
first sums by stable cluster identity and then forms the outer products. Multiway clustering
and serial dependence require their own covariance constructions.
   Cross-fitting has the same constraint. A fold assignment must be a durable function of
the permitted sampling unit or time block, fixed before worker scheduling. A retry must not
duplicate a score contribution; repartitioning must not move a household between training
and evaluation. Floating-point reductions may differ across orders, so a declared numerical
tolerance is appropriate, but the statistical partition must be exact.
   The resulting qualification sequence is constructive. First verify a small finite-law functional
and its failure cases. Then compare the adapter’s actual target and outputs against a numerical
reference. Next evaluate sampling bias, coverage or policy regret under named experiments.
Finally measure the same scientifically valid computation under larger loads, including memory,
spill, retries and cost. A larger row count is useful only after these identities are preserved.


17.9      What the comparison assigns to the shared product
The reusable layer should own the intervention and observation representations, target-
preserving transformations, identification evidence, inference requirements and immutable
execution records. Existing libraries can then supply well-defined numerical operations.
A bounded first set includes adjustment-based effects, valid linear-IV moments, specified
panel/cohort contrasts, finite-horizon observed-history policies and graph-equivalence discovery
outputs. Controlled latent models require a separate observational/interventional likelihood
interface and evidence for the requested value; supplying a planner alone cannot complete it.
    This division also provides a substantive alternative to building the product. An expert
team can compose the same open-source libraries directly. The shared product has value only
if it preserves the scientific contracts more reliably, reduces repeated data and validation work,
and improves decision throughput at a measured total cost. An estimator wrapper with a
common name adds little. The next design step is to specify the exact operations, invalid
requests, numerical obligations and reusable artifacts that make that claim testable.
Chapter 18

Survey method and the common
causal software contract

18.1     Compare a scientific operation before comparing a pack-
         age
A bank considering a causal library faces several different purchasing and engineering decisions.
It may need a defensible effect of an invitation, a description of plausible causal directions
among funding variables, or a policy for repeated servicing decisions. A package that produces
a directed graph does not necessarily answer the first question. A package that estimates an
average treatment effect does not necessarily answer the third. The survey therefore takes a
scientific operation as its unit of comparison: an input with a declared observation law, a causal
target, assumptions connecting the two, and an output whose meaning survives conversion
into the bank’s units.
   This choice changes what counts as competitive capability. Consider a request to increase
deposit funding by changing the offered rate. A system that returns several compatible
effects has provided useful information if the observations cannot distinguish their underlying
mechanisms. A system that returns one number after choosing a convenient graph may have
answered a more restrictive question. The comparison must expose the restriction before
comparing accuracy, speed or convenience. Similarly, a symbolic expression for an effect and
an estimate of that expression are different accomplishments. The expression identifies what
information is needed; its numerical evaluation adds statistical and computational obligations.
  The proposed common request is

                                  q = (U, T , O, A, Y, Ψ, G, S),                           (18.1)

where U specifies the eligible population and sampling unit, T the decision and measurement
clocks, O the observed variables and their units, and A the feasible intervention. Y specifies
the outcome and horizon. The functional Ψ is the requested causal quantity; G contains the
graph or graph class and its substantive restrictions; S describes sampling and uncertainty.
For example, one row may represent one independently sampled eligible customer, the action
may be a 25 basis point increase offered before account opening, and the outcome may be
net funding value over the next quarter. These declarations are scientific inputs. A software
interface cannot establish them merely by accepting a table with suitable column names.
  For an observational law P and an admissible model class M, define
                                                       obs
                          IΨ (P, M) = {Ψ(M ) : M ∈ M, PM   = P }.                          (18.2)

                                               162
18.2. A bounded survey that can be extended without changing its claims                        163


This is the collection of target values compatible with the same observations and assumptions.
It is a population object. A finite-sample graph estimate, an estimated collection of effects, a
Bayesian posterior and a confidence set each add different operations to it. A common result
schema must distinguish these objects. Reducing all four to a scalar and two bounds would
make the schema convenient at the cost of its scientific meaning.


18.2      A bounded survey that can be extended without changing
          its claims
The landscape has two dimensions that should be searched separately. The method dimen-
sion includes observational, latent-variable and interventional discovery; identification and
counterfactuals; heterogeneous effects; instrumental variables and discontinuities; longitudinal
treatment and survival; policy evaluation; panels and differences in differences; synthetic con-
trols; time series; interference; mediation and sensitivity; transport and missingness; Bayesian
structural models; observation construction; and computational workflow. The implementation
dimension distinguishes R, Python, Java, C/C++, other language paths and commercial
offerings. A language binding, an underlying numerical engine and a commercial wrapper can
occupy different positions in that matrix without being three independent implementations.
   The publication cutoff is 7 October 2026. Acquisition time, software revision, manual
generation date and scholarly publication date are retained separately. This matters even for
apparently simple documentation: the inspected pcalg manual identifies version 2.7-12 and a
package date in 2024, while the manual itself was generated in May 2026. The bnlearn manual
identifies version 5.2.1 dated 17 July 2026. BiDAG’s inspected manual was generated in May
2026 but describes a release dated May 2023 (pcalg contributors, 2026; Marco Scutari and
contributors, 2026; Polina Suter and Jack Kuipers, 2026). None of these dates alone measures
current support quality, future maintenance or compatibility with the proposed product.
   A reproducible search records the query, source, date filter, returned identities, pagination
and stopping rule. For the R observational-discovery comparison developed here, the retained
bibliographic query was “R package causal discovery constraint score continuous DAG.” Its
saved first page contains ten records from a reported 1,648 matches. The primary comparison
starts from the inspected pcalg and bnlearn manuals, follows the BCDAG lead, and then
follows one package-reference step to BiDAG and mcmcabn. Those five paths define the
present comparison. Ten bibliographic results are not an exhaustive R census. The remaining
methodological leads do not establish either the presence or the absence of an R implementation.
   There are two useful stopping rules. A discovery pass can stop after a declared search budget
and report incomplete coverage. A capability decision must instead stop when the evidence is
sufficient for the particular claimed operation, or report that the decision remains unresolved.
The first rule controls search cost; the second controls the strength of the conclusion. Conflating
them would allow an arbitrary search budget to become evidence that a missing capability
does not exist. Conversely, insisting on an unbounded census before discussing any inspected
package would prevent useful comparisons indefinitely.
   Each included path needs a canonical identity, exact source or release, license information,
local source bytes, a digest, inspected technical anchors and a claim tied to those anchors.
Scholarly arguments use the original technical text, preserved as a real paper. Software behavior
uses the relevant manual or source. Search metadata establishes identity and discovery, not
algorithmic properties. A summary prepared by the project can explain a source but cannot
substitute for an unavailable original. An unavailable candidate remains visible with its
unresolved claim and the evidence needed to revisit it.
164                                                             Causal analysis for a universal bank


  Conflicting evidence also requires a dated resolution. The authentic BCDAG preprint from
2022 is useful for its Gaussian model and posterior construction. Its contemporary package
comparison cannot determine what bnlearn supports in 2026. The inspected bnlearn manual
now documents intervention and counterfactual operations (Federico Castelletti and Alessandro
Mascaro, 2022; Marco Scutari and contributors, 2026). The sensible conclusion is that the
comparison changed with the software. This does not establish the validity of any particular
causal use of bnlearn; it corrects a capability description at a named version.


18.3      What the five R paths actually return
The five packages illustrate why language and algorithm labels are insufficient. Table 18.1
compares their documented outputs. It is a source-based comparison, not a benchmark of
their implementations.

           Table 18.1: Selected R paths and the distinction their outputs require.
